issues.legal_issue: Vicarious liability for an offence committed by an unlawful assembly requires the accused to be a member of the assembly when the offence is committed.
material_facts: The accused was inside the house where the victim was taken for only a short time and then left; he was not present when police entered the house.
The victim died from strangulation, but the evidence did not establish that the strangulation occurred before the accused left.
The evidence did not rule out that the strangulation occurred after the accused had left and ceased to be a member of the assembly.
issues.conclusion: The accused’s conviction for murder with the aid of unlawful-assembly liability was set aside, and he was acquitted of that charge.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, the prosecution must establish that the accused was a member of the unlawful assembly when the offence was committed. The section imposes liability where an offence is committed by a member in prosecution of the assembly’s common object, or is one the members knew was likely in prosecution of that object. A person who has left and ceased to be a member before the offence is committed is not vicariously liable for a later act of the remaining members. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.

predicates.appeal_from_unlawful_assembly_liability_: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a conviction imposed on the basis of an accused’s membership in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.accused_left_assembly: The accused left the place where the assembly was acting before the authorities arrived.
predicates.fatal_offence_not_shown_to_precede_depar: The evidence does not establish that the fatal act occurred before the accused left, and permits the possibility that it occurred afterward.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges liability based on unlawful-assembly membership, the accused left, and the fatal offence is not shown to have preceded that departure, the conviction based on that liability is set aside.
